scenes.title: Navigating the File System
scenes.narration: Moving around the file system means knowing where you are, seeing what is nearby, and stepping into other directories with confidence.

scenes.title: The Three Questions
bullets: Where am I? — pwd prints your current location so you never get lost.
What is here? — ls shows the files and folders in your current directory.
How do I move? — cd changes directory to wherever you want to go next.
scenes.narration: Almost all navigation boils down to three questions. Running pwd answers where you are by printing the full path of your current directory. Running ls answers what surrounds you by listing files and folders. And cd answers how to move, carrying you into whichever directory you name.

scenes.title: Absolute vs. Relative Paths
scenes.narration: An absolute path begins at the root slash and spells out the full route, so it works no matter where you currently stand. A relative path is shorthand that starts from your current directory. Learning to switch between the two is what makes navigation feel effortless.

scenes.title: Getting Around
scenes.code:
pwd                 # /home/data
cd reports          # move into reports/
cd ..               # go up one level
cd ~                # jump home
cd -                # back to previous dir
scenes.narration: The double dot means the parent directory, so cd .. always steps you up one level. The tilde is a shortcut to your home folder, and cd with a dash flips you back to wherever you just were. These small aliases save an enormous amount of typing over a day.

scenes.text: pwd, ls, and cd are your compass — with them you can find and reach any file on any machine.
scenes.narration: These three commands form a reliable compass. Combined with an understanding of absolute and relative paths, they let you reach any file on any system.
